To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the spatially resolved photoluminescence images are determined by the spatial positions of the excitation and collection, the microscope setup and the spatial distribution of the exciton density.
the microscopic theory of spatially-resolved photoluminescence can model the impact of the experimental setup and the impact of interface fluctuations on spatially-resolved PL images.
the spatial resolutions in photoluminescence experiments can be significantly improved by the use of a microscope with a high numerical aperture and by using the illumination-collection mode.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of microscopic models for the simulation of spatially resolved optical experiments in quantum structures.
the microscopic theory of spatially and spectrally resolved photoluminescent experiments.
the microscopic theory of the spatially resolved photoluminescence of quantum wells with interface roughness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the microscope setup and the illumination-collection geometry are of crucial importance in the interpretation of spatially resolved low temperature photoluminescence experiments.
the spatial resolution of the photoluminescence is determined by the spatial resolution of illumination and collection optics, and not by the spatial resolution in the quantum structure itself.
spatially resolved photoluminescence imaging is a very powerful tool for the investigation of quantum structures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the microscope setup is a very important part of the experimental setup and should be taken into account in a microscopic theory of spatially-resolved experiments.
the microscopic theory of spatially-resolved photoluminescence is a powerful tool for analyzing spatial inhomogeneities in quantum well systems.
spatially resolved photolunimescence images are not necessarily a direct image of the quantum structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial resolution of photoluminescence imaging experiments is not limited by diffraction.
the resolution in the spatially resolved photoluminescence images can be much better than the resolution of the optical microscope.
the resolution of the photoluminescence images is limited not by the microscope but by the spatial inhomogeneity of the quantum well.
